title: Recursion Foundations
relevance: Interviewers use recursion to check base cases, call-stack reasoning, recurrence/complexity analysis, and whether you can trade recursion for iteration when stack depth and overhead matter.

phases.goal: Establish what recursion is, how the call stack works, and what makes a recursive function valid.

must_hit.point: Recursion defines a function in terms of itself using a base case that returns a direct answer and a recursive case that shrinks the problem toward that base case.
must_hit.evidence_hint: Names both parts and says the recursive step must reduce size until the base case fires.

must_hit.point: Each self-call pushes a call frame with locals and parameters; a return pops the frame and resumes the caller, so space is O(depth) of the call tree.
must_hit.evidence_hint: Mentions push/pop of frames and space proportional to maximum recursion depth.

must_hit.point: No valid base case, or a recursive case that does not shrink toward it, causes infinite recursion and a stack overflow when the call stack runs out of memory.
must_hit.evidence_hint: Links missing/broken termination to endless calls and stack overflow.

must_hit.point: Reason with a recursion tree and 'trust the recursion': assume the subcall solves the subproblem, then combine that result for the current problem; time is often a recurrence such as T(n) = T(n-1) + O(1).
must_hit.evidence_hint: Says assume the subproblem is correct and can write a simple linear recurrence for time.

probes: What two parts must every valid recursive function have, and what goes wrong if either is missing or wrong?
How does the call stack behave on a recursive call and a return, and what does that imply for space?

hints.1: Think about stopping versus continuing the self-calls.
hints.2: Base case returns immediately; recursive case shrinks; each call gets its own stack frame.
hints.3: Base case + shrinking recursive case; frames push/pop; bad termination → infinite recursion → stack overflow; space O(depth).

phases.goal: Distinguish how recursive calls are arranged: tail vs head, linear vs tree, indirect, nested, and parameterised vs functional state.

must_hit.point: Tail recursion makes the recursive call the last action with no work after return; head/non-tail recursion still has work after the call returns (e.g. printing before vs after the call).
must_hit.evidence_hint: Defines last-action vs post-return work and can contrast the two print orders.

must_hit.point: Linear recursion makes one recursive call (a line of calls); tree recursion makes multiple recursive calls so the call stack branches.
must_hit.evidence_hint: Contrasts single-call chain with multi-call branching like Fibonacci-style trees.

must_hit.point: Indirect/mutual recursion is when A calls B and B calls A; nested recursion passes a recursive call as the argument to another recursive call.
must_hit.evidence_hint: Separates mutual A↔B from nestedRec(nestedRec(...))-style argument nesting.

must_hit.point: Parameterised recursion builds the answer downward via an accumulator parameter; functional recursion builds the answer upward by combining returned sub-results.
must_hit.evidence_hint: Says accumulator goes down the chain versus combining return values on the way up.

probes: How do you tell tail recursion from head recursion, and what changes about when side effects run?
What is the difference between parameterised recursion and functional recursion when carrying state?

hints.1: Ask whether anything runs after the recursive call returns.
hints.2: Tail = last action; head = work after return; param passes accumulator down; functional combines on the way up.
hints.3: Tail: call is final; head: e.g. print after return; linear vs tree by call count; param accumulator down vs functional combine up.

phases.goal: Surface recursion-versus-iteration costs and when naive tree recursion is too expensive.

must_hit.point: Interviews often expect discussion of recursion versus iteration, especially stack-depth limits and call overhead, and rewriting iteratively to remove O(N) auxiliary stack space.
must_hit.evidence_hint: Mentions stack limits/overhead and dropping O(N) recursion stack by iterating.

must_hit.point: Naive tree-recursive Fibonacci recalculates the same subproblems across the tree, giving O(2^n) time and motivating memoization/DP; space is O(n) for tree height.
must_hit.evidence_hint: Calls out redundant subproblems, exponential time, and DP/memo as the fix; space from max height.

must_hit.point: Choose parameterised recursion when accumulating downward is clearer, or functional recursion when combining returned sub-results upward fits the problem.
must_hit.evidence_hint: Picks the pattern based on whether the answer is built going down or combined coming up.

probes: When would you rewrite a recursive solution iteratively, and what complexity term are you usually trying to remove?
Why is the plain recursive Fibonacci a poor final interview answer?

hints.1: Compare stack usage and repeated work.
hints.2: Iteration avoids deep stacks; Fibonacci tree recomputes overlapping subproblems.
hints.3: Recursion vs iteration: depth limits/overhead and O(N) stack; naive Fibonacci is O(2^n) time from redundant calls → memo/DP.

phases.goal: Apply base/recursive cases and parameterised or functional patterns to standard linear and tree-recursive problems.

must_hit.point: Print 1 to N with a parameterised counter i growing to N, or with head recursion that prints N only after printing 1 to N-1; both are O(N) time and O(N) stack.
must_hit.evidence_hint: Describes either style and states O(N) time and stack space.

must_hit.point: Sum of first N: parameterised path adds into a downward sum; functional path returns n + sum(n-1) with base 0 → 0; both O(N) time and O(N) space.
must_hit.evidence_hint: Shows both styles and O(N) time/space.

must_hit.point: Factorial is functional n * (n-1)! with base 0! = 1; use a wider integer type because factorials grow very fast.
must_hit.evidence_hint: States the recurrence, base 0! = 1, and overflow risk for small N.

must_hit.point: In-place reverse swaps left/right then recurses inward until left meets or crosses right; palindrome compares ends (or s[i] vs s[n-i-1]) and recurses inward.
must_hit.evidence_hint: Two-pointer shrink for reverse; outer-to-inner or index-pair check for palindrome.

must_hit.point: Fibonacci translates F(0)=0, F(1)=1, F(n)=F(n-1)+F(n-2) into tree recursion with base n ≤ 1, at O(2^n) time and O(n) space.
must_hit.evidence_hint: States the recurrence/bases and exponential time with linear stack height.

probes: Walk through printing 1 to N with head recursion versus a parameterised counter—what happens on the way down and up?
How would you reverse an array or check a palindrome recursively with two endpoints?

hints.1: Pick one classic problem and name its base case first.
hints.2: Linear problems: shrink n or move indices; Fibonacci branches to n-1 and n-2.
hints.3: Print/sum/factorial: O(N) stack patterns; reverse/palindrome: meet-in-middle indices; Fibonacci: tree recursion O(2^n) time.

tradeoffs.strong_answer: Recursion mirrors the problem structure and call stack, but interviews push on stack-depth limits, call overhead, and rewriting iteratively to eliminate O(N) auxiliary stack space.

Parameterised recursion passes an accumulator down the call chain; functional recursion combines sub-call return values on the way up—choose based on whether the answer is built going down or composed coming back.
Tail recursion’s recursive call is the last action (no post-return work); head recursion still runs logic after the call returns, which changes side-effect order such as print-before vs print-after.
Pure tree recursion recomputes overlapping subproblems for O(2^n) time; memoizing repeated results is the Dynamic Programming next step, while space stays O(n) from recursion height.

gotchas.trap: Writing a recursive function with no valid base case, or a recursive step that does not shrink toward the base case.
gotchas.correction: Every path must reach a base case that returns directly; otherwise you get infinite recursion and a stack overflow.

gotchas.trap: Treating naive recursive Fibonacci as an acceptable final solution.
gotchas.correction: It is exponential O(2^n) from redundant subproblems; call that out and move toward memoization/DP (and note O(n) stack height).

gotchas.trap: Ignoring stack cost when analyzing recursive solutions.
gotchas.correction: Space is driven by maximum call depth (often O(N) for linear recursion); interviewers may ask you to simulate the stack or rewrite iteratively.

gotchas.trap: Using a narrow integer type for factorial.
gotchas.correction: Factorials grow extremely quickly, so use a wider type (e.g. long long) even for relatively small N; base case is 0! = 1.

gotchas.trap: Confusing when work runs relative to the recursive call.
gotchas.correction: Tail recursion does the call last; head recursion does work after return—e.g. printing before the call yields N..1, printing after yields 1..N.
